headline: U.S. economy added 165,000 jobs in October, showing surprising strength
author: Lauren Kaori Gurley

paragraphs.text: The U.S. economy added 165,000 jobs in October, shattering expectations and suggesting strength in the labor market, especially for white-collar, health care and manufacturing workers.
The unemployment rate ticked down to 4.1 percent, extending low levels that have defined the labor market over the past year, according to a Labor Department report released Friday.
The labor market was stronger than originally reported in August and September, the report showed, with job gains revised up by 84,000 positions for those months.
Wage growth continued to be outpaced by inflation, in bad news for households.

The rosy job figures were unexpected, as soaring prices fueled by the Iran war, tariffs and immigration enforcement have dampened employers’ hiring plans this year. But spending by wealthier households flush with stock market gains has been propping up the economy.

“Today’s jobs report is a strong rebuttal to fears that the economy is heading into a meaningful slowdown,” wrote Seema Shah, chief global strategist at Principal Asset Management, in an analyst note. She added, “Job creation remains broad-based, pointing to an economy that is still absorbing labor comfortably rather than one beginning to buckle under tighter financial conditions.”

The White House, reeling from Tuesday’s midterm Republican wipeout, touted the job gains as a sign of a vigorous labor market. On CNBC, White House National Economic Council Director Kevin Hassett called jobs number “through the roof.”
It’s “as good of a job market as you’re likely to see,” Hassett said.

But strong job gains appeared to have little impact on the stock market, which opened slightly higher Friday morning, after tumbling Thursday in reaction to concerns about whether country’s rapid AI build-out would continue with Democrats in power.
Jobs gains were spread across health care, professional and business services, manufacturing, and transportation and warehousing.

Professional and business services added 70,000 jobs, raising hopes of new growth in white-collar jobs. The sector averaged monthly job gains of around 15,000 over the prior 12 months. The job growth is welcome news for recent college graduates who have struggled to find work this year amid signs that artificial intelligence is zapping entry-level jobs.

The transportation and warehousing sector added 25,000 jobs, mostly delivery workers. Retailers and logistics firms are preparing for a robust holiday shopping season, with Amazon recently announcing the hiring of 300,000 workers for the season.

And manufacturing added jobs for the fifth straight month, including in metal production, which could be one of a few areas benefiting from the president’s tariffs. Manufacturing employers have added 101,000 jobs since hitting a recent low in December 2025.
Leisure and hospitality, and the federal government shed jobs.

Despite some pockets of job growth, many employers are still reluctant to bring on new workers. This year’s average monthly gains are much smaller than the average monthly jobs numbers added just a few years ago. During the first 10 months of 2026, job growth has averaged 86,000 positions per month, compared to the average monthly gain of 210,000 in 2023.

Indeed, there are underlying signs that many Americans are struggling in their job searches. The average duration of unemployment hit more than 27 weeks in October, the highest level since late 2021. Nearly 2 million Americans have been unemployed for more than half a year, the data showed, as new job opportunities are scarce in many sectors, especially in entry-level white-collar positions.

Recent college graduates are facing the brunt of this pain. The so-called underemployment rate for recent college graduates has risen to the highest rate since October 2020, according to data released Monday by the Federal Reserve Bank of New York. Underemployment measures the share of graduates working in jobs that typically do not require a bachelor’s degree.

Another dark spot is workers’ paychecks. Average hourly earnings grew to $38 an hour in October, an increase of 3.1 percent on an annual basis, the most recent data shows — well below inflation at 3.7 percent in September.

Many middle- and lower-income Americans have been feeling gloomy about the labor market and the economy, as war-fueled inflation outpaces workers’ wage gains eroding their spending power. That helps explain why Americans viewed the state of the economy as the top issue in midterm elections, in which voters delivered a wholesale rejection of President Donald Trump and his policies on Tuesday.

“What’s dragging the economy down right now is stubbornly high inflation driven by war in Iran and the shock to energy prices,” said Andrew Flowers, chief economist at Appcast. He added, “It’s also the long-standing structural in-affordability of health care and housing and premiums on health care rising quickly.”

But there are new data shows signs that the labor market could be picking up. In September, workers were quitting their jobs at the highest rate in over a year, according to the job openings report released Tuesday, signaling that some workers are newly confident in their ability to find better employment opportunities. Job openings also rose to the highest level since November 2024, and layoffs remain very low.
